source.title: When Is a Steerable Concept Representation Real? Measurement Confounds in a Cross-Family Audit of Neuroscience Parallels in LLMs
source.authors: Yu-Qi Wu; Shengming Zhao; Jie Chen

page_placements.theme: Neuron concept labels, selectivity and interpretability scores depend on the method

record.tranche_reason: The study audits LLM concept steering, number tuning, language localization, and geographic decoding, but does not measure whether individual neurons respond to several unrelated inputs or test polysemanticity.
record.gate_note: The single-neuron concept-selectivity and number-tuning findings concern related but different constructs: neither tests mixed responses to unrelated inputs. The language-lesion and steering results likewise do not measure polysemanticity. The two closest single-neuron results are recorded as findings that fit none of the claim versions.
record.test_reason: The study audits concept steering, number-neuron tuning, language lesioning and world-map decoding across 17 LLMs. It never measures whether neurons respond to several unrelated inputs. Superposition and dictionary learning are cited only as a warning that decodable directions need not be computational units. No version is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct, with additions. The authors conclude that neuroscience-parallel claims need comparable measurements and controls. The apparent emergence of concept steerability with scale is an artifact of raw units, readout metric and operating point; with controls, steering is significant at every scale with no detectable trend. The linear world map is consistent across all 17 models. The 'monotonic number code' reflects selection bias. The language double dissociation is not robust to bootstrap and attribution-method changes.
record.recipe_differences: The study does not reproduce or directly test a polysemanticity measurement.
record.method_sensitivity: For its adjacent number-tuning analysis, whether units appear bell-shaped depends on neuron-selection criterion. This is not a test of polysemanticity measurement sensitivity.

fits_no_version.finding: Strong number-magnitude tuning appears in all 17 models. Bell-shaped units appear only under shape-agnostic selection; linear selection returns none.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: LLM MLP neurons show number-magnitude tuning whose apparent shape depends on the neuron-selection criterion.

fits_no_version.finding: Single-neuron concept selectivity roughly halves out of sample (d′ ≈ 6 to ≈ 2), with several concepts below the pseudo-concept null. Clamping a top concept neuron degrades output rather than inducing the concept.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In-sample single-neuron concept selectivity overstates held-out selectivity, and selective single neurons are not sufficient causal levers.

record.problems: The study does not directly test the catalog claim. Its dense steering scale analysis is limited to the Qwen3 lineage up to 14B; the authors also note that the 24-concept steering set limits precision and that family and scale effects are not fully separable.
record.rows_left_out: No rows for the four main experiments' steering, language-lesion, and world-map results: they do not measure polysemanticity or the mixed-response behavior in the claim.

untested.parts: No share of MLP neurons responding to unrelated tokens or contexts is measured, and there is no layer comparison of polysemanticity.
Initialization, regularization and noise as causes are not examined.
No activation-function, architecture or regularization comparison of polysemanticity.
No reanalysis of canonical polysemantic neurons.
Measurement dependence is shown for tuning shape and language attribution, not for polysemanticity classification.

record.verdict_notes: Changed the relation from 'discusses' to 'cites_only': superposition (Elhage et al., 2022) appears in a single related-work sentence and is not discussed further. There are no verdicts because no version is tested.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not test polysemantic responses in vision models or InceptionV1.
It does not measure whether a large share of transformer MLP neurons respond to unrelated tokens or contexts.
It does not test whether superposition or capacity pressure causes polysemanticity.
It does not test whether initialization, regularization, or training noise causes polysemanticity without capacity pressure.
It does not compare architectures or activation functions for polysemanticity, or test whether polysemanticity can be reduced without substantial performance loss.
It does not investigate whether canonical polysemantic neurons detect one shared feature or related offshoots of one job.
It does not test whether the classification of neurons as polysemantic depends on activation range or explanation scoring.

rows.subject: all 17 tested models (aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Measured single-neuron number tuning; compared shape-agnostic selection with linear-correlation selection.

conditions.value: numbers 1–40, presented as digits and spelled-out words

rows.measure: Held-out number-tuning correlation and tuning-curve shape
rows.value: The best number-tuned neuron reached held-out r = 0.68–0.98 in all 17 models; bell-shaped units were present in every model under shape-agnostic selection.
rows.note: Aggregate findings about number tuning; they do not establish whether the neurons respond to unrelated input types.
rows.check: Concerns number-magnitude tuning of single neurons. The baseline is a neuron-selection comparison (linear vs quadratic criterion), not a control for mixed selectivity. It is not a polysemanticity measure.

rows.subject: representative model (not named)
rows.operation_detail: Compared in-sample and held-out single-neuron concept selectivity.
rows.value: out-of-sample d′ ≈ 2; several concepts fell below the pseudo-concept null
rows.note: The text gives this as a representative-model result and does not name the model. It concerns generalization of concept selectivity, not responses to unrelated inputs.
rows.check: The subject model is not named ('a representative model'). The row measures concept selectivity in sample vs held out (d′ ≈ 6 to ≈ 2), not responses to unrelated inputs. The state is relative to in-sample selectivity, not to any claim version.

tranche.reason: It never measures whether neurons respond to several unrelated inputs. The single-neuron result is about whether concept selectivity generalizes, not about polysemanticity.

source_check.notes: The neuron result is a two-sentence remark in §4.1 ('The causal reading'), on one unnamed representative model, with no table or CI. It concerns concept selectivity, not polysemanticity. 'Roughly halves' is the authors' word, though d' 6 to 2 is closer to a drop of two-thirds.
